album: Steamin' with the Miles Davis Quintet
label: Prestige
rationale: The fourth and last of the four LPs Prestige assembled from the Miles Davis Quintet's two 1956 Van Gelder dates, and the one still missing from this canon — Cookin', Relaxin' and Workin' are all already in. Independent listing traditions rate it at the level of its siblings: Penguin Guide 4 stars, DownBeat 4.5 stars on release (DownBeat's 1961 reviewer: 'a must for anyone seriously interested in jazz'), AllMusic 5 stars, Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide 4 stars, Encyclopedia of Popular Music 4 stars — all recorded in the Wikipedia album article's ratings table. AllMusic files it as Hard Bop and calls it possibly the best single demonstration of this quintet rebuilding standards ('Surrey with the Fringe on Top', Monk's 'Well, You Needn't', Gillespie's 'Salt Peanuts'). Session gravity is the strongest argument of all: this is the First Great Quintet — Davis, Coltrane, Garland, Chambers, Philly Joe Jones — caught as a working band playing its book, and its absence leaves a literal hole in the middle of the canon's most-documented run. It still plays: blues-drenched, unhurried, and immediately legible to a listener sent in cold.

personnel_record.notes: Two sessions: May 11, 1956 produced 'Surrey with the Fringe on Top', 'Salt Peanuts', 'Something I Dreamed Last Night', 'Diane' and 'When I Fall in Love'; October 26, 1956 produced 'Well, You Needn't'. Those same two dates also yielded the takes released as Cookin', Relaxin' and Workin'. Release year 1961 follows the DB's convention for this set (Cookin' 1957, Relaxin' 1958, Workin' 1960 are all filed by release year, not by the 1956 recording dates). Duration source: Wikipedia track table (40:00 total, matching AllMusic's 39:55). Album-level personnel only for the rhythm section; no per-track credit differentiation was found beyond Coltrane's two sit-outs. Credits also list reissue personnel (Nick Phillips reissue supervisor, Joe Tarantino/Phil DeLancie remastering) — excluded as non-original.

ballot.album: Miles Davis — Steamin' with the Miles Davis Quintet (1961)
ballot.case_for: This is a load-bearing document of the First Great Quintet: Davis, Coltrane, Garland, Chambers, and Philly Joe Jones transforming standards and bebop repertoire into a working-band language, documented at session and track level by S3. AllMusic awards five stars (S2), while S1 reports strong ratings from Penguin, DownBeat, Rolling Stone, and the Encyclopedia of Popular Music, although those assessments are mediated through Wikipedia rather than directly consulted. The contrast between the ballad intimacy of "When I Fall in Love," the drive of "Salt Peanuts," and the ensemble interpretation of "Well, You Needn't" gives the album substantial discovery value independent of its historical status. Its standing alongside Cookin', Relaxin', and Workin' supports completing a foundational recording cycle on musical merit, not merely collecting the fourth title.
ballot.case_against: With three albums from the same two 1956 sessions already represented, Steamin' offers less incremental stylistic and historical discovery than a distinct recording project; this is shared-session redundancy, not duplication of their performances. Its delayed assembly and 1961 release make it a retrospective document rather than a new statement of Davis's contemporary direction, and completing the four-LP sequence is not itself a canonical criterion. The dossier establishes personnel and reception more firmly than album-specific influence: most ratings are reported secondhand through S1, and no cited source directly documents later musicians treating this particular LP as formative.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes that John give Steamin' must-have priority as a consensus-core candidate on its own musical and documentary merits, rather than on sequence completion alone.
